units.translation: Of this preposition (as I said in my Lexicon Sophocleum p. 145) there was from the earliest times a twofold spelling, εἰς [into] and ἐς [into], about which what the Greek grammarians have handed down, though not sufficient, yet two of their observations survive that are not useless. One of them is that of Helladius in Photius' Bibliotheca p. 573, 10: ὅτι ἀναλογώτερον ἀντὶ μὲν τῆς εἰς προθέσεως τὸ ἐς λέγειν, ἀντὶ δὲ τῆς ἐξ τὸ ἐκ· πᾶσα γὰρ πρόθεσις βραχυκαταληκτεῖν θέλει [that it is more analogical to say ἐς instead of the preposition εἰς, and ἐκ instead of ἐξ; for every preposition wants to end in a short syllable]. And p. 535, 2: ὅτι οἱ Ἀττικοὶ κατά τι πάτριον ἔθος οὐ χρῶνται τῇ ει διφθόγγῳ ἐν τῷ λέγειν ἐς κόρακας ἢ ἐς μακαρίαν, ἀλλ᾽ ἄνευ τοῦ διχρόνου ἐκφωνοῦσι τὴν πρόθεσιν· ἐπὶ δὲ τῶν ἄλλων ἁπάντων καὶ μετὰ τοῦ διχρόνου καὶ χωρὶς τοῦ διχρόνου τὴν πρόθεσιν λέγουσιν [that the Athenians, according to some ancestral custom, do not use the diphthong ει in saying ἐς κόρακας [to the crows] or ἐς μακαρίαν [to blessedness], but pronounce the preposition without the long vowel; but in all other cases they say the preposition both with and without the long vowel]. The other is that of the grammarian (in the Epimerismi Homeri) in Cramer's Anecdota Oxoniensia vol. 1 p. 172, 3: ἐς πρόθεσις παρὰ τῷ ποιητῇ συμφώνου μὲν ἐπιφερομένου ἐκβάλλειν τὸ ἰῶτα λέγεται, φωνήεντος δὲ ἐπιφερομένου φυλάττει [the preposition ἐς in the poet is said to drop the iota when a consonant follows, but to keep it when a vowel follows]. “ἀλλ᾽ ἐς μὲν Μενέλαον (Od. 3, 317).” [but to Menelaus] “ἐσβάντες κνήμας τ᾽ ἠδὲ λόφον (Il. 10, 573).” [having gone up onto the shins and the ridge] “εἰς Ἀγαμέμνονα δίον (Il. 7, 312).” [to noble Agamemnon] “εἰς ἐμὰ δέμνια βάντε (Od. 8, 296, ubi nunc recte τὼ δ᾽ ἐς δέμνια | βάντε).” [going into my bed] μάχεται τὸ ‘οἵδ᾽ αἰψ᾽ εἴσβαινον (Od. 9, 103),” [the phrase 'these quickly went on board' conflicts] εἰ μὴ ἄρα οὐκ ἦν παράθεσις, ἀλλὰ σύνθετον· ἀμφίβολον τὸ “εἰς ὄρος ἡ εἰς κῦμα (Il. 6, 347).” [unless it was not a juxtaposition but a compound; the phrase 'to the mountain or into the wave' is ambiguous] ἀναγινώσκεται γὰρ καὶ ἐς κῦμα.” [for it is also read as 'into the wave']. The authority of inscriptions is of no help, since they offer examples of both spellings and are inconsistent, as L. Dindorf said in the Thesaurus vol. 3 p. 298, and the inscriptions later published by Rhangabe and others show the same inconsistency. The same must be said of the manuscripts, in which although both spellings alternate so much that the writers themselves seem to have written now εἰς now ἐς at random, yet in the midst of this inconsistency traces of a sounder principle remain, from which, if the observations of the grammarians I just mentioned and the indications found in the meters of the scenic poets are applied, some rules can be found by which the use of each form is governed. 1. The examples in the tragic poets are of three kinds: in some the meter requires εἰς, in others ἐς, in others either form is allowed. And in Aeschylus indeed, when the meter requires εἰς, it is read in the senarii Pr. 236 361 1028. Sept. 255 1050. Pers. 183 326. Ag. 510 1207. Ch. 299 680 712. Eum. 763. Suppl. 882. Fr. 165 196 236, in the trochaic verse Pers. 230, in the anapaests Pr. 191 1074 1078. Ag. 1464, in the lyrics Pr. 689, (where in a dochmiac I restored εἰς for ἐς from the apograph for ἐς ἀκοὰν ἐμάν [to my hearing]), in the antispasts Sept. 860. Suppl. 538, in the Ionic verses Pers. 67 97, in the glyconics Ag. 384 435. Ch. 612. Eum. 364, in the iambic-cretic verse Suppl. 103. On the other hand, ἐς is required by the meter in the senarii Pr. 2 302 387. Pers 833. Ag. 737. Eum. 56 459 851. Suppl. 330. Fr. 252, in the anapaests Pers. 2, in the dochmiac Sept. 240. The same must be said of verbs compounded with εἰς, which we have all placed under εἰσ-, although the meter sometimes requires εἰς, sometimes ἐς. But of the third kind, the number of examples of each form is almost equal in M, when placed before consonants, both in the simple preposition and in verbs compounded with it, now εἰς now ἐς, for example ἐσβέβηκε [has entered], ἐσθορεῖν [to leap in], ἐσκόμιζε [was bringing in], but rarely is ἐς placed before vowels without metrical necessity. 2. It is well established that Aristophanes and the other comic poets never used the form ἐς when the meter required it, except where they were repeating the words of the tragedians or imitating their style: led by this, Elmsley judged that ἐς was entirely foreign to the usage of the comic poets and that εἰς should be written everywhere, before vowels as well as consonants, an opinion which is opposed not only by the observation of Helladius mentioned above, who no doubt used an older authority, but also by the authority of the manuscripts. For the manuscripts of Aristophanes, whose reliability in orthographic matters is somewhat greater than that of the manuscripts through which the plays of the tragedians have been transmitted, offer the form ἐς in the simple preposition and in verbs compounded with it so often before consonants that the number of examples is almost the same as that of the other form. 3. Therefore, comparing these indications with each other, I proposed in my Oxford annotation on Arist. Ach. 242 vol. 3 p. 385 the following rule: "the distinction between εἰς and ἐς in the comic poets is that εἰς is written before vowels, ἐς before consonants. The usage of the tragedians departs from this rule only in that ἐς is also said before a vowel where metrical necessity demands." Meineke in his Leipzig edition of Aristophanes of 1860 and others agreed with me, but others disagree, who have no alternative but to follow the example of the scribes and believe that the ancient writers wrote now εἰς now ἐς at random. Nor does the opinion that some have held, that certain words, such as εἰσφορά [tax], which is found consistently written thus in inscriptions, or classes of words, such as ἐπεισπίπτειν [to fall upon], ἐπεισφέρειν [to bring in upon], and other such double compounds, are exempt from my rule, even if it could be true in general, have much appearance of truth, since the reason for this distinction is not apparent and the number of examples is very small. Whether the writers themselves had such great care that they never departed from the rules they had set for themselves, and never placed εἰς before consonants either by chance or for the sake of euphony, and, what is less credible, never placed ἐς before vowels without metrical necessity, cannot be known, since the manuscripts discredit themselves not only by their inconsistency, but also by sometimes introducing εἰς and ἐς against the law of the meter. As for euphony or metrical elegance, the opinion of some is very uncertain that in senarii, and especially in the third dipody, ἐς Ἴλιον [to Ilium], ἐς αὔριον [to tomorrow], ἐς ὕστερον [to later], ἐσείδομεν [we saw] and all such forms are more probable than those which offer a spondee, εἰς Ἴλιον [to Ilium], εἰς αὔριον [to tomorrow], εἰς ὕστερον [to later], εἰσείδομεν [we saw].
